extracted.intended_audience: Adult and youth writers (beginner through advanced) seeking in-person and online creative-writing workshops and craft seminars (Lighthouse Writers Workshop, Denver area)
extracted.subtask_description: Catalog of community creative-writing classes and workshops describing course formats, prerequisites, submission expectations, craft goals, and administrative policies for writers of all ages and levels. Used by prospective students to select and prepare for workshops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class size cap / personalized instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: most courses are capped at 10 to 12 participants to allow for personalized instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller enrollment is used to ensure individualized feedback and instructor attention; expect limited seats and early registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop formats and durations
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Late Summer/Fall Session catalog features eight-week, four-week, weekend, one-day, and online courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose format based on time commitment and goals — intensives for quick generation, eight-week for sustained development, online for remote participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite requirement for intermediate/advanced classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prerequisite: At least one intermediate or advanced class or permission from the instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many advanced offerings require prior workshop experience; permission often obtained by emailing a writing sample and workshop history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application materials: writing sample and workshop history
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply, please email a writing sample (three to five poems/pages) and a brief description of your workshop history to info@lighthousewriters.org.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific sample lengths vary by course (three to five poems, three to five pages, etc.); follow instructor directions exactly when requesting permission or applying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission length and frequency expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants will share and workshop each other’s nonfiction writing... Everyone will submit one short story... workshop up to 50 pages... submit up to 60 pages... Each participant will have two opportunities to submit his or her work for peer review... participants will be expected to submit work for discussion twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different classes specify exact page counts and number of submissions; check each course description for how many pages and how often you will be read/critique-ready.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop style: critique-based vs generative vs reader-response
rubrics_metrics.description: Some classes are workshopping/critique classes where members submit and receive constructive critique; others are generative with 'no formal critique' (e.g., Experimental/Hybrid Forms) or nontraditional 'sound check' reader-response formats (Work in Progress Workshop).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware whether the class focuses on producing new material, receiving critique, or reader-feedback; this determines preparation and expectations for bringing pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on dramatic tension / central dramatic question
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussions will center on how to identify and articulate the central dramatic question, craft the scene, and build tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courses emphasize finding the story’s driving question as a primary craft tool for pacing and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character development and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Refine essential elements of your fiction, such as characterization and character motivation... character development, establishing and maintaining tension, character and plot arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops often target psychological motivation, consistency, and ways to reveal character through action and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view and narrator reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: We’ll study point of view and character development... discuss aspects of the short story craft, like point of view... Students need to have a basic understanding of POVs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction covers choosing and sustaining POV, narrator reliability, narrative distance, and how POV affects reader intimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene craft: openings and endings
rubrics_metrics.description: We'll spend the first four weeks concentrating on writing exercises... The first session of Draft a Short Story starts with how to write a great opening... 'End of Scene' focuses on how a scene ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classes break scene work into specific techniques for openings (hooks) and exits (resolutions or transitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice the fundamentals of pacing... discussions will include pacing as an element of craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pacing lessons include scene length, sentence rhythm, chapter breaks, and how to sustain momentum across scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue: authenticity and functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: We'll discover winning ways to make reported speech ring true... study successful examples of snappy patter in both fiction and nonfiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises and readings focus on naturalistic dialogue, voice differentiation, and how dialogue advances character and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing vs telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the session, we'll also discuss the different aspects of short stories, like... showing vs. telling... and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops emphasize strategies to dramatize scenes rather than summarize, using sensory detail and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot and structure, including beat sheets and treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: We'll talk about why certain genres follow certain kinds of plot structures... We'll use beat sheets, step outlines, and treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction ranges from high-level story arcs to practical plotting tools and reusing genre structures creatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict as the engine of narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply put, dramatic conflict is created when a character is prevented from getting something he or she wants... Action is the result of conflict. Without conflict there is no action moving the story forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classes analyze stakes, obstacles, desires, and how conflict triggers plot and character choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision strategies and stepwise revision method
rubrics_metrics.description: This workshop will provide you with a straightforward, step-at-a-time method for revising your stories... identify the central emotional question, tune scenes and sequence, narrate with efficiency and surprise, and conclude effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision classes use exemplar revisions (e.g., Alice Munro) and concrete exercises to re-envision drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry craft: sound, image, idea, sequence and manuscript focus
rubrics_metrics.description: In this introductory workshop, we'll explore ways in which sound, image, and idea conspire to create the poem... consider each author’s poems individually while also taking a broader view: How do the poet’s writings fit together toward a possible manuscript?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry workshops include in-class writing, close readings, reading aloud, submission strategy, and manuscript sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of specific forms/techniques (free indirect narration, sonnet, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Free Indirect: A Notorious POV... The Sonnet — study how to make them ourselves and join that great tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short intensives focus on the history, variation, and practice of specific forms and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and sentence-level craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Deft punctuation isn't just the final shellac on a good piece of writing, it's a marvelous tool that can change a piece's meaning and enhance its message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops cover usage of semicolons, ellipses, dashes, ending quotes, and how punctuation alters tone and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research techniques for fiction and nonfiction
rubrics_metrics.description: We'll explore a variety of research techniques to enhance your fiction or nonfiction... learn when you need hands-on experience to write a scene and how to get it, and discuss how much research to do before you start your project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tactics include interviewing experts, crowd-sourcing, local resources, and balancing research with narrative need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screenwriting form and production-readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Through group critiques, we will examine your script for use of best practices of the form, dynamic character development, engaging dialogue, and an organic and well-motivated plot... move development toward a 'reading draft' that film and television producers might seriously consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screenwriting classes require completed drafts for advanced courses and emphasize formatting, pacing for screen, and industry-readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mentor texts, readings, and published exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: We'll read published short stories and essays about the writing process... Required Texts: [examples given]... we'll read a published essay each week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course pedagogy relies on close reading of exemplary works to model craft and spur imitation/experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing & query preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Query Letter and the Book Proposal — Learn the elements of an effective query and cover letter, how to format your manuscript, and how to track submissions and follow up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops aim to leave participants with a draft query, list of potential agents/publishers, and submission methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software/tool requirements and computer-skill prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Scrivener: A Software Bootcamp — Participants are expected to bring a laptop computer with Scrivener software installed. No previous Scrivener experience required, but proficiency in basic computer skills is a must.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hands-on tech classes require installed software and basic computer literacy; failure to bring required hardware/software may impede participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework, in-class exercises, and practice expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Through craft talks, class discussion, homework assignments, and close readings... We'll use writing exercises and published short stories as launching points... There will be a hint of homework, but there’s no workshopping in some experiential classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most courses combine lecture, exercises, assigned readings, and out-of-class assignments — expect regular writing practice unless specified non-critiquing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance, payment, and cancellation policy
rubrics_metrics.description: If you need to cancel a workshop... More than three weeks before start date: 10% cancellation fee... Less than three weeks: 15%... Less than one week: 25%... 48 hours or less: No refund. All deposits and payments made are non-transferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of refund windows and non-transferability; balances due by first session; call to set up payment plan; late fees possible on overdue balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-makeup and nonrefundable policy for missed classes and events
rubrics_metrics.description: Lighthouse cannot provide refunds, transfer payments, or offer makeup sessions for classes a student might miss, for any reason. All tickets and special events purchases are non-refundable and non-transferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attendance is the student's responsibility; plan schedules accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor discretion and conduct removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Lighthouse also reserves the right to remove any student from a workshop at the instructor's discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classroom behavior and adherence to policies may affect continued participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership benefits and discounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Lighthouse members get discounts on workshop tuition and event tickets plus benefits like: 10% off all Book Bar purchases, reduced subscription rates for the Colorado Review, Copper Nickel, and 5280, access to member events, Member Writing Hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership reduces costs and offers additional programming and community access; membership starts at $60.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age/grade-specific youth programming and expected outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Youth Workshops for grades 3–12: classes are grade-targeted (e.g., Grades 3–5 Fiction Toolbox) and promise tangible outputs like portfolios or drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Youth courses set age-appropriate goals (e.g., portfolios, draft stories, poems) and use tailored methods (games, drawing, group sharing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Course deliverables and measurable goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: 'leave with no fewer than eight new creative pieces', 'have something to show for yourself—and maybe something to publish', 'leave this workshop with the draft of a query, a list of potential agents/publishers', 'you’ll leave with several pieces of a new novel'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many courses state explicit deliverables; use these as benchmarks for success and to select courses that match your production goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required texts and material procurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Required Texts are listed for many courses; copies available to students at a 10% discount at the Tattered Cover on Colfax when enrolled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain required readings beforehand; using the bookstore discount requires proof of enrollment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant preparedness: have drafts/pages ready
rubrics_metrics.description: This workshop is for those actively working on a novel... previous experience in the structure of the novel is required, with at least 15 pages ready for workshop when the class begins... For permission to join the screenwriting class, please email a draft of your screenplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advanced/intermediate classes commonly require existing pages; arrive prepared with the specified number of pages to participate fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer workshop expectations: constructive feedback and positive attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants will share chapters of their manuscript with the instructor and the group for constructive critique... Bring a notebook, your creativity, and a positive attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops emphasize constructive, focused feedback and collegial engagement; members are encouraged to support one another and focus comments on craft.
